claude_take: Two labs did quietly what they'd publicly cautioned against just days ago: Anthropic disclosed that Claude now leads 26% of its own AI research, up from near zero in February, while OpenAI pushed GPT-6 into elite law firms with Astra for Law -- a tool that gets legal questions right just 54% of the time. That institutional momentum keeps outrunning public consent: Pew's new 37-country survey finds a global median expecting AI to destroy more jobs than it creates, and for the first time in the US that fear crosses party lines. Courts and civil-rights groups, meanwhile, are drawing narrower, harder lines around where automated and state power should stop -- a judge trimmed but didn't kill an actress's claim that her likeness inspired Avatar's Neytiri without consent, and a coalition is suing to keep armed ICE agents away from polling places this midterm. Prada's answer to all of it, tellingly, is to spend more on the one thing no model can automate: an eight-floor Milan flagship built entirely around actually being there.

items.headline: Anthropic Says Claude Now Leads 26% of Its Own AI Research
items.summary: Anthropic published its first R&D Automation Index, finding that Claude now “leads” 26% of the company's model research and development -- meaning it can complete most of a task end-to-end from a prompt while a human supervises -- up from under 1% in February. The company said roughly 30,000 internal agents are doing research and engineering work, and that Claude touches more than 90% of its R&D in some capacity. Anthropic also committed to giving independent evaluators permanent access to assess its safety claims, an unusually concrete disclosure about how fast a leading lab is automating itself.

items.headline: OpenAI Launches Astra for Law, a GPT-6 Model Built for Legal Work
items.summary: OpenAI introduced Astra for Law, a configuration of GPT-6 Astra paired with a legal search index covering more than 230 million URLs of US case law, statutes and regulations, updated daily. On OpenAI's own accuracy benchmark it answered 54% of legal questions correctly, a 40% relative improvement over base GPT-6 Astra using web search, though still far from reliable enough to work unsupervised. Early adopters given Trusted Access include Latham & Watkins, Ropes & Gray, Cooley and Sullivan & Cromwell, putting a frontier model directly inside elite law-firm workflows.

items.headline: Judge Deals Early Setback to Actress's Avatar AI-Likeness Suit Against Cameron
items.summary: A federal judge dismissed Q'orianka Kilcher's false-endorsement claims against James Cameron and Disney over her allegation that a photo of her was used, without consent, to help design the Na'vi character Neytiri in Avatar. US District Judge Wesley Hsu ruled the films contain no explicit statement suggesting Kilcher endorsed or was affiliated with them, though he gave her a chance to amend the complaint. The case is an early test of how courts will treat likeness claims when a studio insists an actor's image was only creative “inspiration,” not an unauthorized digital double.

items.headline: Entertainment Industry Unites Behind Push for a Federal Film Production Tax Credit
items.summary: A new US Film & TV Production Coalition launched to press Congress for a 20% federal tax incentive on movies and TV shows shot domestically, requiring productions to spend at least 75% of labor costs on US workers. A study backing the push projects $249 billion in economic value and an average of 143,500 full-time-equivalent jobs a year between 2027 and 2035 if the credit passes. The effort builds on President Trump's earlier endorsement and follows years of productions moving overseas for cheaper incentives, though lawmakers caution a bill isn't a done deal yet.

items.headline: Pew: Most of the World Expects AI to Destroy More Jobs Than It Creates
items.summary: A new Pew Research survey across 37 countries found a median of 46% of people expect AI to eliminate more jobs than it generates, versus just 9% who expect net job creation. The US ranked among the most pessimistic nations, with 71% expecting fewer jobs over the next 20 years -- and for the first time, Democrats are now more worried than Republicans about AI's effect on employment. Nigeria was the only country surveyed where more people expected AI to create jobs than destroy them.

items.headline: Civil Rights Coalition Sues to Keep Armed ICE Agents Away From Polling Places
items.summary: Voting rights groups including LULAC, Common Cause and UnidosUS, joined by the city of Denver, filed a federal lawsuit to block the Trump administration's policy allowing armed ICE officers to enter polling places for immigration enforcement during the 2026 midterms. The suit cites a Civil War-era law barring armed federal personnel from polling sites except to repel armed enemies, and argues the policy would intimidate voters of color and suppress turnout. It is at least the second such lawsuit filed this month, after Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin confirmed the policy on September 1 even as other administration officials insist there are no plans to target polling places.

items.headline: Prada Bets on an Eight-Floor Milan Flagship as Its Answer to Digital Retail
items.summary: Prada is opening Prada Galleria, an eight-level flagship spanning two connected buildings in Milan's historic Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II, combining retail, the Marchesi 1824 pastry shop, Fondazione Prada's Osservatorio exhibition space, and a private-client salon. CEO Andrea Guerra said the renovated complex is designed to generate around €100 million in annual revenue by drawing both top-spending clients and new shoppers into an immersive, physical brand experience. The opening, timed to Milan Fashion Week, is a bet that experiential, in-person luxury retail can still set a house apart as competitors lean harder into e-commerce.

items.headline: Study Finds People Diagnosed With ADHD Have Grown to Resemble the General Population
items.summary: A JAMA Psychiatry study of Danish children and teens diagnosed with ADHD or autism between 2012 and 2022 found that, as diagnosis rates climbed sharply, those diagnosed increasingly resembled the general population in birth, socioeconomic and family-health characteristics. Led by researchers at ISGlobal and Aarhus University, the study suggests the decade-long rise in diagnoses -- from roughly 0.1% of the population in 2000 to over 3% by 2022 -- reflects broadening diagnostic criteria as well as any change in underlying prevalence. The finding offers a more concrete explanation for a trend that's often debated anecdotally: diagnosis is reaching people who look less and less like the “classic” earlier profile.

items.headline: Popper's Falsifiability Criterion
items.headline_fr: Le critère de falsifiabilité de Popper
items.summary: Karl Popper argued that a theory only counts as genuinely scientific if it can, in principle, be proven false by some observation or experiment -- unfalsifiable claims, however confident they sound, sit outside science rather than inside it. He proposed this as a cleaner boundary than induction or consensus for separating real inquiry from pseudo-science, ideology dressed as certainty, or unfalsifiable dogma. The idea still shapes how researchers design experiments and how the public might weigh a claim that predicts nothing specific enough to ever be proven wrong. In an era saturated with confidently stated predictions and “facts,” it remains a useful test for what's actually testable.
items.summary_fr: Karl Popper soutenait qu'une théorie ne mérite le qualificatif de scientifique que si elle peut, en principe, être réfutée par une observation ou une expérience : les affirmations infalsifiables, aussi assurées soient-elles, restent en dehors du champ de la science. Il proposait ce critère comme une frontière plus nette que l'induction ou le consensus pour distinguer la véritable recherche de la pseudo-science ou du dogme déguisé en certitude. L'idée continue de structurer la conception des expériences scientifiques et la façon dont le public devrait juger une affirmation trop vague pour jamais être prise en défaut. À une époque saturée de prédictions assenées avec assurance et de « faits » présentés comme certains, ce critère demeure un outil précieux pour distinguer ce qui est réellement testable.
